01: Ford introduces the Model T. Simple, tough and cheap, it put America on wheels; more than 15 million were built by 1927.
Japan opens the Tokaido Shinkansen between Tokyo and Osaka, the world's first high-speed 'bullet train' line, days before the Tokyo Olympics.
02: In London, John Logie Baird transmits the first television picture of a recognizable human face: office boy William Taynton.
03: The first successful V-2 rocket launch, at Peenemunde, Germany, climbs about 50 miles high. Its designers later built America's moon rockets.
04: The Soviet Union launches Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite. Ham radio operators around the world tuned in to its beeps.
05: The World Series is broadcast on radio for the first time; Grantland Rice covers the games for Pittsburgh's KDKA.
06: The Reno Gang robs an Ohio & Mississippi Railroad train near Seymour, Indiana: the first robbery of a moving train in the United States.
07: The Washington, the first double-decker steamboat, arrives at New Orleans: the pattern for the Mississippi riverboats that followed.
Soviet probe Luna 3 photographs the far side of the Moon, the first look at the half never seen from Earth.
08: On the same dry, windy night the Great Chicago Fire starts and the Peshtigo Fire in Wisconsin kills more than 1,200, the deadliest wildfire in U.S. history.
09: Joshua Stoddard of Worcester, Massachusetts, patents the steam calliope, soon the loud voice of riverboats and circus parades.
10: President Wilson presses a telegraph key in Washington, setting off the blast that breaches the Gamboa dike and floods the Panama Canal's Culebra Cut.
11: Apollo 7 launches: the first crewed Apollo flight, and the first live TV broadcast from an American spacecraft.
12: Columbus's expedition makes landfall in the Bahamas after more than two months at sea.
13: The Continental Congress votes to fit out two armed vessels: the birth of what became the U.S. Navy.
14: Capt. Chuck Yeager flies the Bell X-1 'Glamorous Glennis' faster than the speed of sound over the Mojave Desert.
15: The airship Graf Zeppelin lands at Lakehurst, New Jersey, completing the first transatlantic flight by an aircraft carrying paying passengers.
16: The Nickel Plate Road (the New York, Chicago and St. Louis Railroad) runs its first trains over its whole 513-mile line from Buffalo to Chicago.
17: The Radio Corporation of America (RCA) is founded, keeping American radio patents in American hands after World War I.
18: Texas Instruments and Regency announce the TR-1, the first commercial transistor radio. Price: $49.95.
19: George Pullman dies in Chicago. His sleeping cars set the standard for overnight rail travel.
20: Gen. Douglas MacArthur wades ashore on Leyte, keeping his promise to return to the Philippines.
21: Nelson's fleet defeats the French and Spanish at Trafalgar; Nelson is killed aboard HMS Victory.
22: Andre-Jacques Garnerin makes the first parachute jump from a balloon, about 3,200 feet above Paris.
23: Apple introduces the iPod: '1,000 songs in your pocket.'
24: The first transcontinental telegraph line is completed. The Pony Express shuts down two days later.
25: Off Samar, the escort carriers and destroyers of 'Taffy 3' turn back a far larger Japanese fleet in the Battle of Leyte Gulf.
26: The Erie Canal opens, linking the Great Lakes to the Hudson River and New York City.
27: New York City's first subway line opens, run by the Interborough Rapid Transit Company (IRT).
28: Ironworkers set the final section of the Gateway Arch in place, completing St. Louis's 630-foot arch.
29: The first message crosses ARPANET, the internet's forerunner, from UCLA to Stanford. 'LOGIN' crashed after 'LO'.
30: Orson Welles's 'War of the Worlds' on CBS radio convinces some listeners that Martians have landed in New Jersey.
31: A German U-boat sinks the destroyer USS Reuben James off Iceland: the first U.S. Navy warship lost in WWII, five weeks before Pearl Harbor.
